issues.legal_issue: Credible testimony from close relatives may establish the identity and participation of the assailants despite the witnesses’ relationship to the deceased.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were close relatives of the deceased, and one lived in a neighbouring village.
The eyewitnesses said an electric light at the tubewell enabled them to identify the appellants, whom they already knew.
One eyewitness promptly reported the assailants to the police, and his account was corroborated by the person to whom he first reported the incident and by the medical evidence.
The courts below scrutinised the eyewitnesses’ evidence and accepted it.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship to the deceased did not make their testimony unreliable; the evidence was sufficient to sustain the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: Relationship to a deceased person does not, by itself, disqualify a witness or make the witness’s testimony unacceptable. Such testimony must be scrutinised, and may be relied upon when credible and supported by the circumstances and corroborative evidence. The Court found no infirmity in the concurrent findings of the courts below.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and related_witnesses_testified and witnesses_knew_the_accused and identification_conditions_supported_recognition and testimony_was_corroborated

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused challenged their convictions in an appeal.
predicates.related_witnesses_testified: People related to the deceased testified as eyewitnesses.
predicates.witnesses_knew_the_accused: The eyewitnesses were acquainted with the people they identified as assailants.
predicates.identification_conditions_supported_reco: The witnesses described circumstances, including available light, that enabled them to see and identify the assailants.
predicates.testimony_was_corroborated: The eyewitness account was supported by other evidence, including a prompt report, testimony about the first disclosure, or medical evidence.

issues.definition: When an appeal against conviction involves related eyewitnesses who knew the accused, had conditions supporting recognition, and gave corroborated testimony, that testimony can support the conviction.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to examine an eyewitness does not, in the circumstances of this case, undermine other eyewitness testimony where the reason for the omission was accepted and the objection was not raised at the earliest opportunity.
material_facts: A witness who was sleeping near the deceased was not examined, and the prosecution said he had been won over.
The investigating officer had recorded a further statement from that witness implicating two people who were later acquitted as falsely involved.
The defence did not challenge the stated reason for the witness’s non-examination before the courts below.
The two examined eyewitnesses had already unfolded the prosecution’s account.
issues.conclusion: The non-examination of the witness did not reflect on the credibility of the two examined eyewitnesses.
issues.legal_principle: Dropping a witness on an unsupported assertion that the witness was won over is generally to be frowned upon. However, the Court, referring to Sahaj Ram v. State of U.P., [1973] 1 SCC 490, held that the omission did not warrant undermining the other eyewitnesses in these circumstances: the reason was accepted below, no timely objection was raised, and their testimony unfolded the prosecution’s case.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and an_unexamined_witness_was_present and the_reason_for_nonexamination_was_accepted and no_timely_objection_was_raised and examined_witnesses_unfolded_the_case

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused challenged their convictions in an appeal.
predicates.an_unexamined_witness_was_present: A person who could have witnessed the occurrence was not called to testify.
predicates.the_reason_for_nonexamination_was_accept: The courts accepted the explanation given for not calling that person.
predicates.no_timely_objection_was_raised: The defence did not raise the complaint about the witness’s absence before the courts below when it could have done so.
predicates.examined_witnesses_unfolded_the_case: The witnesses who testified gave the account needed to present the prosecution’s case.

issues.definition: When an appeal against conviction concerns an unexamined witness, an accepted explanation, no timely objection, and other witnesses who unfolded the case, the omission does not undermine those other credible witnesses.

issues.legal_issue: An omission to obtain a medical opinion about whether a particular weapon could cause an injury does not undermine credible direct testimony when the witnesses explain how the weapon was used.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses said that a blow to the deceased’s chest was delivered with the blunt side of a cutting weapon.
The doctor described the chest injury as an abrasion caused by a hard and blunt object but was not specifically asked whether the blunt side of that weapon could have caused it.
The eyewitness account was accepted and was corroborated by other evidence.
issues.conclusion: The failure to elicit the doctor’s specific opinion did not render the direct testimony doubtful or weak.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution should endeavour to ask the medical witness whether an injury could have been caused by the alleged weapon, and the presiding officer should elicit that opinion where appropriate. Under Hallu and others v. State of M.P., [1974] 4 SCC 300, and the Court’s discussion of Nachhattar Singh and others v. State of Punjab, [1976] 1 SCC 750, a witness’s clarification that the blunt side was used may prevail over the ordinary inference about how such a weapon is used. Kartarey v. State of U.P., [1976] 1 SCC 172, and Ishwar Singh v. State of U.P., [1976] 4 SCC 355, were relied on regarding the need to elicit medical opinion; the omission did not weaken credible direct evidence in this case.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and eyewitnesses_described_blunt_side_use and medical_evidence_showed_blunt_force_injury and doctor_was_not_asked_about_the_specific_weapon and direct_testimony_was_credible

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused challenged their convictions in an appeal.
predicates.eyewitnesses_described_blunt_side_use: The eyewitnesses said that the blunt side of the weapon was used to inflict the injury.
predicates.medical_evidence_showed_blunt_force_inju: The medical evidence described the relevant injury as one caused by a hard and blunt object.
predicates.doctor_was_not_asked_about_the_specific_: The doctor was not specifically asked whether the alleged weapon, used in the described manner, could have caused the injury.
predicates.direct_testimony_was_credible: The court accepted the eyewitnesses’ account as credible.

issues.definition: When an appeal against conviction involves credible direct testimony describing blunt-side use and medical evidence of blunt force, the omission of a specific question to the doctor does not undermine that testimony.

issues.legal_issue: Contradictions drawn from witness statements fabricated to implicate people falsely do not have evidentiary value against the witnesses’ testimony.
material_facts: The courts below found that the investigating officer had fabricated statements attributed to the eyewitnesses to implicate two people who were not named in the first report and were later acquitted.
The fabrication was found to have been made to explain the presence of those people in police custody after they had been illegally detained.
The informant promptly told the police that those people were wrongly detained and later filed an affidavit alleging fabrication.
There was no evidence that the officer who reviewed the investigation had countersigned the statements used for contradiction.
issues.conclusion: The contradictions based on the fabricated statements had no evidentiary value and did not show that the prosecution had shifted its case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the concurrent factual finding that the statements attributed to the witnesses had been fabricated. Contradictions based on those statements therefore could not be used to discredit the eyewitnesses. The Court considered the statements recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in reaching that conclusion.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused challenged their convictions in an appeal.
predicates.witness_statements_were_found_fabricated: The courts found that statements attributed to witnesses had been deliberately fabricated.
predicates.fabrication_was_used_to_implicate_unrela: The fabricated statements were used to involve people whom the prosecution’s initial account had not named.
predicates.the_claim_of_fabrication_was_promptly_ra: A witness promptly complained that the statements were fabricated and that the people concerned were wrongly implicated.

issues.definition: When an appeal against conviction involves statements found to be fabricated to implicate people absent from the initial account, and the fabrication was promptly challenged, contradictions drawn from those statements have no evidentiary value.

issues.legal_issue: The alleged motive did not make the prosecution case unreliable where the evidence showed longstanding disputes and the eyewitnesses had no reason to falsely implicate the accused.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on a dispute over the passage of sullage water and on election rivalries between the deceased and the appellants’ group.
Proceedings relating to the sullage-water dispute were pending.
The defence argued that the sullage-water quarrel was too minor and remote to motivate the killing.

The Court found that the election dispute and the water dispute together supplied a sufficient motive and that a weak motive would not explain why the eyewitnesses would falsely implicate the appellants.
issues.conclusion: The motive argument did not undermine the prosecution case, and the earlier cases relied on by the defence did not apply to these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the alleged motive in the full circumstances, including the election rivalry and the dispute over sullage water, and distinguished A.N. Rao v. Public Prosecutor, Andhra Pradesh, [1975] 4 SCC 106, and State of U.P. v. Hari Prasad and others, [1974] 3 SCC 673, as inapplicable to the special facts of the case.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused challenged their convictions in an appeal.
predicates.evidence_showed_multiple_sources_of_host: The evidence disclosed more than one source of hostility between the accused’s group and the deceased.
predicates.eyewitnesses_had_no_apparent_reason_to_f: The evidence disclosed no reason for the eyewitnesses to falsely accuse the appellants.

issues.definition: When an appeal against conviction involves evidence of multiple sources of hostility and no apparent reason for eyewitnesses to falsely implicate the accused, an attack based on the alleged motive does not make the prosecution case unreliable.
